rv.q: The director Ian Rickson steers a wild text and holds Tempest's satirical energy in a truly compelling arc.
Snip 20 minutes from Ian Rickson's characteristically imaginative yet grounded production and this might be a flat-out masterpiece.
The results are variable. As are Tempest's lines: sometimes soaring, sometimes hectoring; sometimes vaporising into abstraction, sometimes peculiar and daring.
I'd sit through this long, uninterrupted 110-minute show all over again, just for Odysseus's brilliant pizza gag.
But if it didn't totally click for me, two hours of exile with these oddballs is never anything less than interesting.
Tempest infuses the play with richness: we hear their poetry and their musicality but it doesn't make a powerful whole.
It's all so rich, so powerful, so triumphantly theatrical and savagely beautiful that it's overwhelming. You need to see it.
For the National's return to performance without social distancing, they have come up with a corker.
But this show is slick and polished, and, most importantly, it has teeth.
Kae Tempest is aiming their bow at too many targets and unfortunately, unlike Philoctetes, a lot of Tempest's arrows miss the bull's eye completely.
This doesn't feel like a work of art but a symptom of mental illness.
Paradise certainly lives up to the hype but it does take some getting used to.

cn.t: Tempest's bold, all-female adaptation of Sophocles divides critics. Most praise Lesley Sharp's extraordinary central performance and the contemporary relevance, though some find the sprawling production uneven and its radical reimagining doesn't fully cohere.
